passage: The lab was noisy with the carpentry class next door, and the team had exactly forty minutes before the bell. Ojas slapped down a pile of sticky notes. “Twenty designs, no judging, go.” Eshaan wrote a six-legged walker, Ojas drew a robot with a fan, someone sketched a wheeled arm that grabbed cans. By 4:15 twenty notes covered the whiteboard. Then Ojas drew three columns: cost, time, skills we have. Everyone stuck dots. The six-legged walker got lots of dots for excitement and none for time. The simple line-follower with three sensors angled to look ahead of the wheels won on all three. “Simple, but with a clever sensor layout,” Eshaan said. They stuck that note in the middle of the board just as the bell rang.

qa.q: How many designs did the team put on the whiteboard?
What was Eshaan feeling about the winning design?
qa.a: Eshaan was pleased and convinced, since Eshaan called it simple but with a clever sensor layout.

qa.q: What could the team do if the sensor arrangement fails?
qa.a: They could test other sensor angles or fall back to a plainer layout, keeping the simple base that scored well on cost, time and skill.

qa.q: How might the person who proposed the six-legged walker feel?
qa.a: That person may feel disappointed, but the dots gave the idea a fair hearing, so the loss is easier to accept. 🙂

grounding: Team members write twenty possible designs on sticky notes without judging, then vote on cost, time and skill and choose a simple line-follower with a clever sensor arrangement.

passage: In Thomas's flat in Kochi, twenty yellow sticky notes covered the fridge door. Sunaina had set one rule: "No saying 'that won't work' for ten minutes." So the notes said everything: a spider robot, a drone that drops a ball, a line-follower, an arm that sorts coins, a hovercraft. After ten minutes Thomas drew a table on the back of an old calendar: cost, time, our skill. Each idea got a score from one to three in each column. The drone scored high on excitement and one on everything else. The hovercraft lost on cost. "The line-follower's boring," Sunaina said, "but it wins every column." Thomas stared at it. "Unless we make it less boring. What if we put the sensors in a curve, not a straight row? It'd see turns earlier." Sunaina grinned and wrote that on a twenty-first note.

qa.a: No saying that won't work for ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel about the line-follower at first?
qa.a: Sunaina found it dull and called it boring, but was pleased it won every column, and grinned at Thomas's twist.

qa.q: What else could the pair add to their scoring?
qa.a: They could add a column for how easily it can be repaired on the day, so a broken part doesn't end their run.

qa.q: How does Thomas respond to the boring winner?
qa.a: Thomas doesn't just accept it, but finds a clever sensor twist that keeps the safe choice while making it more interesting to build.

grounding: Shows teammates writing twenty robot ideas without judging, scoring them on cost, time and skill, and choosing a simple line-follower with a clever sensor layout.

passage:
The team of four sat around the lab table, a timer on the phone.
"Five minutes. Every idea goes on a note. No judging."
"Robot that climbs stairs."
"Robot that plays chess!"
"Solar car."
"Line-follower."
"Noor, that's so basic."
"Lokesh. No judging. Write it."
Twenty notes later:
"Now we vote. Cost, time, what we can actually build. Three stickers each."
"Stair climber gets two. Chess gets one. Solar car one. Line-follower gets... eight?"
"Because we can build it in six weeks with parts from the lab, and we all know the code."
"But everyone makes a line-follower, Noor."
"Not with the sensors on a little swinging arm in front. It'd see the curve before the wheels reach it."
"...Okay. That's actually clever. Fine. Line-follower with a swinging sensor arm."

qa.q: How many stickers did the line-follower get?
What did Lokesh feel about the line-follower at first?
qa.a: Lokesh was disappointed and a bit scornful, calling it basic because everyone makes one.

qa.q: What would you add to make the vote even fairer?
qa.a: Writing the criteria on the board first and scoring each idea against them openly, so votes reflect cost, time and skill rather than excitement.

qa.q: How might Noor see Lokesh's change of mind?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved and respected that Lokesh called the idea clever once the sensor arm was explained.

grounding: Illustrates a team listing twenty ideas without judging, voting on cost, time and skill, and picking a line-follower with a clever sensor arrangement.
